But I’d just like to point out that logically speaking there are situations where proof of non-existence are possible. I’m speaking about the realm of mathematics and pure logic. For example, take the statement that “No X is a Y.” It means that no member of class X is also a member of class Y. The truth value of this statement is determinable if it is possible to enumerate every single instance of class X and verify that none is also a member of Y. If you can prove that X and Y are completely disjoint classes — that they have no overlap — then the statement is true. Of course, a single counter-example will falsify the statement.

These types of proofs are possible to construct in the world of mathematics but not usually in the real world, unless they follow strictly from definition, in which case they constitute an a priori proof, that doesn’t have anything to do with the exigency and messiness of the real world. Our human definition and ontologies may not always translate into natural categories.

The situation is similar to the notion of a “black swan,” which was originally used as an example of something which could exist but doesn’t actually exist. Until black swans were discovered in Australia. So now we use the term to mean something that is not predictable, following from a book of the same title.
